label: Problem set 5
title: Problem set 5: Basic potential step methods
summary: Practice with chronoamperometry: Cottrell decay, charge passed, sampled current, and the double potential step.

intro.text: A potential step is the simplest controlled-potential experiment. Under diffusion control the current follows the Cottrell equation, i = nFAD^(1/2)C/(pi^(1/2)t^(1/2)), and the charge passed is Q = 2it.
A plot of i against t^(-1/2) is a straight line for diffusion control, and the double potential step lets the product of the first step be examined by the reverse current.

sections.title: Hint sheet: step relations
sections.summary: Practice with chronoamperometry: Cottrell decay, charge passed, sampled current, and the double potential step.

blocks.text: A potential step is the simplest controlled-potential experiment. Under diffusion control the current follows the Cottrell equation, i = nFAD^(1/2)C/(pi^(1/2)t^(1/2)), and the charge passed is Q = 2it.
A plot of i against t^(-1/2) is a straight line for diffusion control, and the double potential step lets the product of the first step be examined by the reverse current.

questions.question: A potential step is applied so a species is reduced under diffusion control. Use the Cottrell equation with n = 2, A = 0.010 cm2, D = 1.0e-5 cm2/s, C = 1.0e-6 mol/cm3, t = 4.0 s. Calculate i in microamperes.
For a Cottrell decay the charge passed up to time t is Q = 2 i t. For the previous step (i = 1.72 uA at t = 4.0 s), calculate Q in microcoulombs.
In a chronoamperometric step the current at 1 s is compared with the current at 4 s. What is the ratio i(1 s)/i(4 s)?
questions.explanation: Since i is proportional to t^(-1/2), the ratio is sqrt(4/1) = 2.0.

questions.question: Chronoamperometry measures:
options: Current as a function of time after a potential step
Potential as a function of time under constant current
Impedance as a function of frequency
Mass as a function of charge
questions.explanation: In a potential step the potential is controlled and the resulting current is recorded against time; the decay is the Cottrell response.

questions.question: After a large enough potential step the surface concentration of the reactant falls to essentially zero.
questions.explanation: When the step puts the electrode into the mass-transfer-limited region, every reactant that arrives reacts at once, so the surface concentration is zero.

questions.question: A plot of i against t^(-1/2) from a potential-step experiment should be:
options: Curved
A straight line through the origin for diffusion control
A horizontal line
A single point
questions.explanation: Because i = (constant) t^(-1/2), a plot of i versus t^(-1/2) is linear; a straight line confirms diffusion control and its slope gives D.

questions.question: In sampled-current voltammetry the current is read at a fixed time after each step. If that time is doubled, by what factor does the sampled Cottrell current change? (Answer as a fraction.)
questions.explanation: i is proportional to t^(-1/2), so doubling t multiplies the current by 1/sqrt(2) = 0.707.

questions.question: A double potential step can be used to detect and study the product of the first step.
questions.explanation: Stepping the potential back oxidises or reduces whatever the first step produced, so the reverse current reports on the product and its fate.

questions.question: Which are true of a diffusion-controlled potential step? Select all that apply.
options: The current follows the Cottrell equation
The current decays as t^(-1/2)
The surface concentration is driven to zero
The current is constant with time
questions.explanation: A diffusion-controlled step gives a Cottrell decay, falls as t^(-1/2), and drives the surface concentration to zero. The current is not constant.

questions.question: The Cottrell slope m = i t^(1/2) is constant. If i = 1.72 uA at t = 4.0 s, what is m in uA s^(1/2)?
The Cottrell current is proportional to t^(-1/2). If i = 1.72 uA at t = 4.0 s, what is i in uA at t = 16 s?
The charge passed up to time t is Q = 2 i t. If i = 1.72 uA at t = 16 s, calculate Q in uC.
In sampled-current voltammetry the current is read:
options: At a fixed time after each potential step
At the moment the step is applied
Only at infinite time
Never
questions.explanation: Reading at a fixed, well-defined time after each step gives a reproducible, diffusion-controlled current that varies with potential like a polarogram.

questions.question: After a potential step the diffusion layer thickness grows with the square root of time.
questions.explanation: The diffusion layer grows as sqrt(pi D t), so the Cottrell current, inversely related to it, decays as t^(-1/2).

questions.question: Which factors determine the Cottrell current? Select all that apply.
options: The diffusion coefficient of the reactant
Its bulk concentration
The square root of time
The colour of the solution
questions.explanation: The Cottrell current depends on D, C and t (as t^(-1/2)), along with n, A and F. Colour is irrelevant.
